sources.title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
sources.author_or_org: D. Sculley; Gary Holt; Daniel Golovin; Eugene Davydov; Todd Phillips; Dietmar Ebner; Vinay Chaudhary; Michael Young; Jean-François Crespo; Dan Dennison
sources.evidence_summary: The primary Google paper identifies ML-specific system risks including boundary erosion, entanglement, hidden feedback loops, undeclared consumers, data dependencies, configuration debt, external-world change, glue code, and pipeline jungles. It argues that the hard maintenance burden is system-level, not confined to model code.
sources.limitations: A 2015 research paper describing Google experience; it predates foundation-model and agentic stacks and does not prescribe organizational reporting lines.
sources.currentness: Stable archival primary publication; official Google Research landing page and paper metadata were live on 2026-08-18.

sources.title: The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness and Technical Debt Reduction
sources.author_or_org: Eric Breck; Shanqing Cai; Eric Nielsen; Michael Salib; D. Sculley
sources.evidence_summary: The primary paper presents 28 production-readiness tests spanning data and features, model development, ML infrastructure, and monitoring, and explicitly treats debuggability, rollback, and monitoring as production duties for trained models.
sources.limitations: The rubric is based on Google production experience and is not a universal compliance standard; teams must adapt thresholds and test depth to consequence and context.
sources.currentness: Stable archival primary publication; official Google Research landing page and paper download were live on 2026-08-18.

sources.title: MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning
sources.author_or_org: Jarek Kazmierczak; Khalid Salama; Valentín Huerta; Google Cloud
sources.evidence_summary: Google Cloud distinguishes exploratory model work from the engineering challenge of integrating and continuously operating an ML system. It describes CI, CD, continuous training, data and model validation, serving, monitoring, retraining triggers, and rollback as one production lifecycle.
sources.limitations: Cloud-architecture guidance aimed primarily at predictive AI; product names and maturity levels are examples, and team boundaries vary by organization.
sources.currentness: Official page states last reviewed 2024-08-28 and was live on 2026-08-18.

sources.title: MLOPS02-BP01 Establish ML roles and responsibilities
sources.evidence_summary: The AWS Machine Learning Lens explicitly separates domain expert, data engineer, data scientist, ML engineer, MLOps engineer, auditor, model-risk, cloud-security, prompt-engineering, and integration functions. It centers the ML engineer on converting prototypes into production-ready software and the MLOps engineer on reusable training, testing, and deployment automation.
sources.limitations: Prescriptive cloud guidance, not a labor-market taxonomy or mandatory staffing model; its ML engineer definition is intentionally concise and organizations may combine roles.
sources.currentness: Part of the AWS Machine Learning Lens published 2025-11-19; section was live on 2026-08-18.

sources.title: 5 AI RMF Core
sources.author_or_org: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.evidence_summary: The NIST AI RMF Core separates govern, map, measure, and manage; requires clear roles, lines of communication, ongoing review, incident processes, and executive responsibility for AI risk decisions. It notes that lifecycle actors often lack visibility or control over other parts of an interdependent system.
sources.limitations: Voluntary, non-sector-specific framework; the page states AI RMF 1.0 is being revised, so later integration must recheck the revision status.
sources.currentness: Official AIRC rendering of AI RMF 1.0 was live on 2026-08-18 and prominently disclosed an in-progress revision.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence overview
sources.evidence_summary: Microsoft documents a shared-responsibility boundary across provider infrastructure and model operations, customer application use and governance, and board, council, policy, research, and engineering functions. Existing privacy, security, accessibility, compliance, and sensitive-use programs retain their formal controls.
sources.limitations: Microsoft-specific assurance documentation with deployment-model-dependent responsibilities; it is not a generic role definition and the page does not expose a reliable publication date.
sources.currentness: Official Microsoft Learn page was live on 2026-08-18; content is operational guidance and may change without a versioned publication date.

sources.title: Good Machine Learning Practice for Medical Device Development: Guiding Principles
sources.author_or_org: U.S. Food and Drug Administration; International Medical Device Regulators Forum
sources.evidence_summary: FDA points to the 2025 IMDRF final GMLP principles for safe, effective, high-quality AI/ML medical devices across the total product lifecycle, preserving the role of regulators, clinical context, and sector-specific evidence beyond engineering implementation.
sources.limitations: Sector-specific medical-device guidance; it should not be generalized into a universal release procedure, and the linked IMDRF document carries the detailed principles.
sources.currentness: Official FDA page and linked final-document reference were live through official indexing and browser inspection on 2026-08-18; the review curl path redirected to Akamai abuse detection and then returned 404.

sources.title: Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy
sources.evidence_summary: OpenAI's public postmortem describes a model update whose individually positive changes combined into harmful sycophancy, while offline evaluations and aggregate A/B signals missed the behavior. It records monitoring, mitigation, full rollback, targeted evaluation gaps, and a commitment to make qualitative and proxy behavior signals launch-blocking.
sources.limitations: A self-reported incident from one consumer LLM product; it does not disclose all internal evidence or transfer unchanged to predictive ML systems.
sources.currentness: Official page content was retrievable through browser verification on 2026-08-18; direct curl received HTTP 403 bot protection without changing the canonical URL.

sources.title: Spotify Technology Career Steps
sources.evidence_summary: Spotify's primary career framework defines progression by widening impact, accountability, business thinking, mastery, cross-team leadership, company-level problem solving, and sustained responsibility rather than by title or a move into management.
sources.limitations: Published in 2016 as Spotify's version-one framework and not ML-specific; useful for durable depth dimensions, not current Spotify level mapping or universal promotion criteria.
sources.currentness: Stable official engineering publication remained live on 2026-08-18; historical status is explicit.

sources.title: Jobs
sources.evidence_summary: Spotify's live employer-controlled index concurrently listed Machine Learning Engineer at senior through senior-staff depth and distinct Data Engineer, Staff Engineer for content-intelligence infrastructure, platform, cloud-security, enterprise-AI, experimentation, and applied/R&D contexts. This is evidence of differentiated families, not universal definitions.
sources.limitations: A volatile snapshot of openings; titles, linked postings, locations, and availability can change or disappear and the index alone does not define each role's formal authority.
sources.currentness: Live employer-controlled index inspected and HTTP 200 verified on 2026-08-18.

sources.title: Staff Machine Learning Engineer, AI
sources.evidence_summary: The employer-controlled Staff MLE posting combines production-grade model and agent development, scaled deployment, major-initiative ownership, documentation, mentoring, and leadership or collaboration across engineers, product teams, and multiple teams.
sources.limitations: One volatile employer posting for an AI-focused role; requirements reflect Sentry's current team and cannot define staff scope for every organization.
sources.currentness: Employer-controlled Ashby posting returned HTTP 200 and remained open on 2026-08-18.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council (Artificial Intelligence Act)
sources.author_or_org: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
sources.evidence_summary: The official regulation assigns distinct obligations to providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems, including provider responsibility, deployer monitoring, competent human oversight, and links to data-protection duties. Legal status attaches to regulated actors, not to an engineering job title.
sources.limitations: Jurisdiction- and risk-class-specific law with staged application, amendments, and interpretive guidance; this research does not provide legal advice or determine whether a particular system is in scope.
sources.currentness: Official EUR-Lex record resolved on 2026-08-18; automated curl returned HTTP 202 and a JavaScript challenge, while the official indexed record exposed the regulation text and metadata.

claims.statement: The durable center of Machine Learning Engineering is converting model or data-science work into a production-ready learning system and owning workload-specific integration across qualification, serving, monitoring, and change; it is not model experimentation alone.
claims.limitations: Organizations may combine model development, ML engineering, and MLOps in one person or team; this claim defines the accountability center, not a universal org chart.

claims.statement: Production readiness requires evidence across data, features, models, pipeline components, serving behavior, monitoring, retraining, and rollback because an ML model can degrade or fail even when conventional code tests and offline metrics pass.
claims.limitations: The required tests, thresholds, monitoring windows, and release controls remain consequence- and domain-specific.

claims.statement: Recurring ML lifecycle failures are system-interface failures: entangled changes, hidden data or feedback dependencies, undeclared consumers, configuration drift, incomplete actor visibility, and individually acceptable changes whose combination creates unsafe behavior.
claims.limitations: The sources establish recurring mechanisms and one public incident, not frequency estimates or a complete failure taxonomy.

claims.statement: MLOps, ML platform, infrastructure, SRE, and security functions own reusable automation, shared runtime or fleet reliability, access boundaries, and cross-workload controls; the Machine Learning Engineer owns the model workload's use of those capabilities and its model-specific operational evidence unless authority is explicitly reassigned.
claims.limitations: Small organizations often collapse these roles, and shared-responsibility boundaries vary with managed-service and deployment choices.

claims.statement: Evaluation and safety must retain an independent release-gate voice: aggregate offline or A/B metrics can miss consequential behavior, so targeted deployment evaluations, qualitative expert evidence, incident processes, and formal risk review can block or reverse a launch.
claims.limitations: The sources do not mandate one universal evaluation organization; independence may be procedural rather than a separate reporting line.

claims.statement: Product, domain, security, safety, privacy, governance, legal, executive, and regulatory authorities retain decisions about purpose, intended use, risk tolerance, compliance, sensitive use, and domain validity; an MLE supplies implementation and evidence but does not unilaterally authorize those decisions.
claims.limitations: Exact authorities depend on jurisdiction, sector, company policy, deployment model, and system risk class; this is a responsibility boundary, not legal advice.

claims.statement: Current practice distinguishes Machine Learning Engineer from data science, data engineering, applied research, platform or infrastructure, security, policy and safety, and generative or agentic specializations; shared implementation does not erase their different decision centers.
claims.limitations: Employer titles are volatile and inconsistent, and the sampled index cannot prove that every organization uses each title or the same boundary.

claims.statement: Advanced and staff-level MLE depth is demonstrated by sustained production ownership, wider cross-team or company impact, ambiguous problem framing, architecture and initiative leadership, business judgment, mentoring, and raising operational standards—not by algorithm novelty or people management alone.
claims.limitations: One source is a historical general technology framework and one is a current AI-focused job posting; level calibration remains employer-specific.
